architecture_context.target_observation: podman top rc=125 because the observed container did not create a cgroup; promotion-bearing container resource telemetry must therefore remain UNKNOWN until repaired or replaced

primary_sources.name: Linux kernel cgroup v2 documentation
relevant_facts: Every process belongs to one cgroup in the unified hierarchy.
/proc/$PID/cgroup in the initial cgroup namespace exposes the real v2 path as 0::$PATH; a process inside a cgroup namespace may see its namespace root as / instead.
cpu.stat accounts cgroup CPU usage; memory.current/memory.peak/memory.events and io.stat are cgroup-scoped interfaces when available.
cgroup.events populated describes whether a cgroup subtree contains live processes.

primary_sources.name: Podman create documentation
relevant_facts: --cgroups=enabled creates a new cgroup under the cgroup parent.
--cgroups=disabled deliberately forces the container not to create cgroups.
Podman supports cgroupfs or systemd as cgroup managers.

primary_sources.name: Podman container inspect documentation
relevant_facts: Container inspection exposes the low-level State structure including the payload PID while running, and exposes the PidFile path.

primary_sources.name: systemd control-group interface and cgls documentation
relevant_facts: systemd services/scopes/slices are mapped onto cgroups and resource-control properties.
systemd-cgls can enumerate the processes and descendant groups of a selected cgroup or unit.

findings.finding: A Podman container can validly have no dedicated cgroup. Therefore the observed podman-top cgroup error is compatible with an intentionally/non-isolating cgroup mode and must not be converted into either a container-resource PASS or a semantic runtime FAIL.

The strongest read-only recovery path starts from the host-observed container payload PID, then resolves that PID's cgroup membership from the host/initial cgroup namespace. Reading /proc/self/cgroup inside the container is insufficient because a cgroup namespace can make the namespace root appear as '/'.

If the resolved host cgroup is a dedicated container/subtree, cgroup-v2 counters can be candidate container-scope resource evidence subject to membership/coverage checks. If the resolved path is a shared parent/systemd scope, the same counters are only SUPERSET evidence: they include other processes/descendants and cannot certify container isolation or exact container resource use. If the path is root or controller files are unavailable, cgroup-scoped resource fields remain UNKNOWN.

systemd-cgls/systemd unit membership is useful as a topology/membership witness, not as a magic attribution oracle. A parent service/scope can prove that the payload is inside a known subtree, but shared-subtree counters remain causally ambiguous until unrelated members are excluded or a dedicated child cgroup is created for a future run.

The existing AgentCgroup donor rule remains correct: exit 137 alone is not OOM proof. memory.events oom/oom_kill can corroborate a cgroup-level OOM event, but under a shared parent it still cannot by itself identify which child caused the event.

bounded_native_design.name: CgroupWitness/v1-candidate
bounded_native_design.purpose: Repair the epistemic gap around missing dedicated-container cgroup telemetry without importing AgentCgroup controller authority.
hard_rules: No dedicated cgroup => do not claim container resource isolation.
Shared parent/scope counters => label SUPERSET, never exact container usage.
Inside-container cgroup path '/' => do not infer host root membership without host-side lookup.
Missing controller/interface => explicit UNKNOWN/UNAVAILABLE, never zero.
Observation never grants or changes budget/capability/effect authority.
No destructive cgroup mutation is required for this read-only witness path.

counterhypotheses.statement: Host-level memory/disk/uptime plus process RSS is already sufficient; cgroup recovery adds no useful promotion discriminator.
counterhypotheses.discriminator: Compare whether a host/parent cgroup witness can establish a stable workload membership boundary and bounded CPU/memory/event counters that process-only telemetry cannot provide; reject the design if all available paths are shared/root and add no attribution.

counterhypotheses.statement: The correct fix is to force every future target run into a dedicated cgroup rather than add fallback observation semantics.
counterhypotheses.discriminator: Treat dedicated-cgroup execution as the preferred future-run configuration when safe/authorized, but keep fallback witness semantics because current/legacy observations and cgroup-creation failures must remain representable without fabricated zeros or PASS.

next_high_information_discriminator.action: On the next non-destructive target-VPS probe, obtain the running payload PID from Podman inspect, read host /proc/<pid>/cgroup, classify the path as dedicated/shared/root/unresolved, enumerate membership, and read only present cgroup-v2 resource files. Persist raw values plus scope/coverage semantics. Do not promote container isolation when scope is shared/root.
next_high_information_discriminator.success: A dedicated or uniquely bounded subtree is observed with stable membership and readable counters, yielding candidate container-scope telemetry.
next_high_information_discriminator.bounded_partial: A shared parent/systemd scope is observed; metrics are retained as SUPERSET evidence only.
next_high_information_discriminator.failure_closed: Host path cannot be resolved, points to root without useful controller files, membership is unstable/ambiguous, or permissions prevent reads => container cgroup telemetry remains UNKNOWN.

promotion_decision.reason: The source review identifies a concrete discriminator and epistemic schema, but no target-runtime E3/E4 evidence has yet shown that the fallback produces unique reliable telemetry on the current VPS. Reusing the existing WP605/AgentCgroup E5 candidate remains preferable to minting a competing implementation lane.
